evidence: Cic. Cael. 59: saepe mē, saepissimē rem pūblicam
terms.comment: The everyday word, of things that happen again and again at intervals; Lewis & Short contrasts crēbrō, of things that come close one after another. How often? is quotiēns? (Traupman 87; see whenever).

evidence: Cic. Att. 7.10.1: crēbrō ad mē scrībe
terms.comment: Of things that come thick and fast (Lewis & Short): letters, coughing, hoeing. The adjective crēber is first thick, close-set (trees, buildings), then frequent.

Not common until after Augustus (Lewis & Short): Quintilian uses it often, and so do Petronius’s freedmen. It also means in great numbers (Liv. 1.11.4). The adjective frequēns is first of people often in a place or often doing a thing (frequēns audītor, a regular hearer), then of things that happen often.

phrases.latin: crēbrō Catulum, saepe mē, saepissimē rem pūblicam nōminābat
phrases.english: he kept naming Catulus, often me, and most often of all the Republic

phrases.latin: tū, quaesō, crēbrō ad mē scrībe vel quod in buccam vēnerit
phrases.english: please write to me often, even just whatever comes into your head

phrases.latin: crēbrō runcātō. simul herbae incēperint nāscī, eximitō
phrases.english: weed often; as soon as the weeds start coming up, pull them out

phrases.latin: nam tam bonae memoriae sum, ut frequenter nōmen meum oblīvīscar
phrases.english: for my memory is so good that I often forget my own name
